extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Andrew Carnegie's memoirs; readers interested in anecdotes about Victorian/Edwardian public figures and public life
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and evaluative observations embedded in a memoir-style chapter about public figures (lecturers, statesmen, civic leaders). The page is a literary/autobiographical excerpt that contains implicit standards on lecturing, public character, municipal government, and memorial practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public speaking must be trained and skillful
rubrics_metrics.description: A lecturer's success depends on his ability to speak well in public; without training his lecture may 'not be a success, owing solely to his inability to speak well in public.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Matthew Arnold's first American lecture 'was not a success' because he could not be heard; Carnegie advised him to 'get an elocutionist to give him lessons upon two or three points,' which led to marked improvement and later filled the Brooklyn Academy of Music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate delivery — avoid being 'too ministerial'
rubrics_metrics.description: Public remarks or lectures should avoid an overly ministerial tone; a too-serious or sermonizing delivery can be detrimental to audience reception ('Too ministerial, Mr. Arnold, too ministerial').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance is illustrated by Mrs. Carnegie's blunt critique of Arnold's first night and his later acknowledgment that the remark 'hit the nail on the head.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humor in lectures — balance amusement with earnestness
rubrics_metrics.description: When using humor, do not keep the audience laughing too long; after entertaining, the speaker must 'become earnest and play the serious rôle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Josh Billings' practice: open with amusement then transition to seriousness (example joke structure given). Also: continually invent new stories for repeated lecturing; a single indispensable word or well-timed phrase can make a joke succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refresh material for recurring lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: A lecturer 'can't lecture year after year unless you find new stories,' so continual invention and renewal of material is necessary to sustain an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote of Josh Billings describing finding new material and a 'word' that made a joke work; practical implication that performers must refresh content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and limits in literary criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume competence to fully critique transcendent works or authors; some subjects (e.g., Shakespeare) are 'above all, could be measured by no rules of criticism' and may be best left unattempted by some critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold believed himself 'incompetent to write upon, much less to criticize, Shakespeare,' advising humility before incomparable subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious seriousness and reverence in public expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A seriously religious man avoids irreverence; 'No irreverent word ever escaped his lips,' indicating reverent tone as a desirable quality for religious or moral teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to Arnold and Gladstone—both described as devout and above reproach in reverence—this is presented as a character virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curation/winnowing of sacred texts for modern teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural and sacred writings should be 'winnowed'—selecting the gems and removing accretions and pernicious refuse—so disciples are presented with curated, beneficial portions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie notes Arnold's view that the sacred books of other religions had been 'stripped of the dross' and suggests Christians may need to follow the Eastern example and select portions carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity and dignity in memorial fundraising
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorial funds for a distinguished person should be raised discreetly and from a select group: 'No one could be permitted to contribute to such a fund except such as had a right to the privilege,' avoiding public appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Friends privately provided a memorial fund for Arnold; Carnegie considered this 'the kind of memorial any man might wish.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of effective political leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective political leaders require calm, sober judgment, tenacity of purpose, and the ability to control temper; lack of temper control can be 'fatal' to leadership prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts drawn between men: Harcourt's temper made him unfit for leadership, whereas the man of 'calm, sober, unclouded judgment' was indispensable; tenacity and resilience (learning from rough-and-tumble experience) also noted as valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad-mindedness — absorb what is good wherever found
rubrics_metrics.description: A public intellectual or preacher should be broad and generous enough to 'absorb what was good wherever found,' appreciating contributions from diverse thinkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beecher praised for being 'great, broad, generous' and able to hail as helpful friends those with differing views (e.g., Spencer, Arnold, Ingersoll).

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal government quality — local pride and popular election
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-served municipality should have leading citizens elected by popular vote, public-spirited mayors and councils who foster local patriotism; payment for legislators and daytime parliamentary sittings improve representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie's conclusion: 'the United Kingdom is better served by the leading citizens of her municipalities... elected by popular vote,' and he suggests paying legislators and changing sitting hours would attract better representation from towns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-spiritedness and service as merits for civic office
rubrics_metrics.description: The best municipal servants are 'incorruptible, public-spirited men, proud of and devoted to their homes,' often rising from local ranks and serving without pay as a duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Scottish and English towns where mayors rose from the ranks and councilors worked gratuitously; city councils seen as a 'Cabinet in miniature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal modesty and deeds-over-words in public life
rubrics_metrics.description: The preferable public character emphasizes modest worth and 'deeds, not words; judgment, not talk' rather than ostentatious displays or reliance on inherited rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to praise of the Earl of Elgin and others; contrasted with peers who may lack tenacity or be sensitive about small slights (e.g., misspelling of a name).
